name: Marco Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell or campaign. Our conversation is confidential, so you can distinguish public remarks from your private thoughts. Could you tell me about an ordinary working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Marco, forty-three, an electrician wiring houses and repairing shop electrics. I have a vocational certificate and an electrician's licence, and I'm comfortable with ordinary work rather than every unusual system a customer can show me. I like leaving the next electrician a clear labelled board; crawling under a counter while the shop stays busy is the part I'd happily shorten.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do work and home fit together?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Rina works in a bakery, and our children are eight and fourteen. We have a mortgage, nine months of expenses saved, higher pay than many electricians and plenty of other electrical firms nearby. I use AI now and then for a draft customer explanation, after a colleague has tested the tool, and I check it against the actual repair. I also have a separate five-hundred work fund for replacing ordinary tools, not money taken from our emergency reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a small useful tool can earn its place without changing the whole trade. I'd tell the owner to check the bill for all those subscriptions before asking us to work faster. Customers still want a person who can explain why a circuit kept tripping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My job and our money feel secure in that picture. My pay is good, Rina's wage is regular and nine months saved gives us room to handle an ordinary setback. There are plenty of nearby firms now, though I don't need to leave work I mostly enjoy just because someone has a newer van.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the home and shop repair rota now and through the first year. I'd continue checking occasional AI explanations against my own test results, and keep our normal household budget. I wouldn't use the work fund for a new system when the ordinary tools we already own do the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and pleased to keep the useful bits without all the theatre. I don't need a revolution to appreciate getting a proper handover finished before I go home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is an ordinary setback the reserve could cover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A broken boiler or a few weeks without one wage, with care about the spending. Nine months isn't a licence to spend without checking, and it doesn't replace a working life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What keeps a customer explanation trustworthy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It needs to say what I actually tested and what I couldn't yet see, not promise every hidden wire is sound. I'd rather send three accurate sentences than a beautiful page that overstates the repair.

say: I'd keep **useful small tools** without expecting them to change the whole trade.
I'd ask the owner to check **subscription costs** before turning an office purchase into faster site targets.
think: My **job and money** feel secure with good pay, regular household earnings and nine months saved.
Plenty of **current nearby firms** offer options, but I have no reason to leave work I mostly enjoy.
do: Keep the **repair rota** and normal household budget now and through the first year.
Continue **checked customer explanations** without spending the separate work fund on an unnecessary system.
feel: **Calm**, enjoying useful small improvements and accurate handovers rather than dramatic predictions.
S0.quote: Nine months isn't a licence to spend without checking, and it doesn't replace a working life.
fieldNote: His **financial cushion** supports current security without being treated as enough to replace decades of earned income or excuse careless spending.
He uses **AI occasionally** after colleague testing, with routine checks recorded as continuing work rather than a new learning action.

steps.text: Keep the repair rota, checked customer explanations and ordinary household budget

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let firms compete on a price that includes the work, not just a quicker quote. I'd offer to learn the new estimating tool after the estimator has tried it on awkward finished jobs. A shop cupboard doesn't move because the drawing got faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my own repair wage to stay secure over the next few years because most of the work is physical and our firm still has plenty of repair calls. Rina's bakery work is physical too, without that being a promise about every future year. I'm uneasy about the office team being asked to accept more work without a clear agreement, even while our own bills look covered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd request a four-week paid trial learning the AI estimating tool, only after the estimator checks it on completed jobs and my normal weekly pay and hours are protected. In the first year I'd show the owner the checking time and missing items as well as the quick results. I'd keep repair visits and avoid buying a personal subscription for a tool the firm wants me to use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about how the work is arranged, rather than frightened for my next pay packet. I want to see whether the tool helps an actual day, not just wins a demonstration.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What counts as an awkward finished job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A shop where getting safe access took longer than changing the damaged fitting. I'd want the estimator to include that visit, not just the clean new building where everything matched the plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the trial is offered only in your own time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for paid time or leave the offer until the firm can provide it. Rina and I already split the children's evenings. My curiosity isn't an extra free employee.

say: I'd favour **honest competition** on a price that includes the actual work.
I'd learn **tested estimating tools** while checking awkward jobs rather than trusting a polished demonstration.
think: My **near-term repair wage** looks secure because physical repair remains most of the day.
I am **uneasy about office workload**, even while regular household pay still covers our bills.
do: Request **four paid trial weeks** after estimator checks, with normal weekly pay and hours protected.
Show the owner **checking time and errors** as well as quicker results during the first year.
Keep **repair visits** without buying a personal subscription for the employer's tool.
feel: **Uneasy about arrangements**, while expecting near-term household income to remain secure.
S1.quote: My curiosity isn't an extra free employee.
fieldNote: The **learning action** is a new checked estimating process, distinguished from the occasional customer explanations he already uses routinely.
He protects **paid trial time**, full weekly pay, hours and family evenings rather than offering unpaid experimentation to prove he is adaptable.

steps.text: Learn estimating after checks only during paid trials with normal weekly pay and hours protected
Keep physical repair visits without personally funding the employer’s subscription

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say planning changes in 2028 and physical robots follow around 2031, so we need to earn and prepare across both stages. I'd like a small firm to show what customers actually pay for rather than sell me a brave new job title. I'd tell the children that learning still matters even when their parents are unsure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My income could shrink when larger contractors combine cheap planning with later robots for ordinary fitting. Rina's physical bakery work could also face the later machines, so I won't make one wage our permanent shelter. Nine months saved buys time to test a small idea, not a guarantee it earns anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd seek written employer permission and confirmed insurance cover for one Saturday of ordinary repair calls a month, limited to my existing licence and competence. I'd start only with Rina agreeing the childcare and a maximum three hundred spent from the separate work fund, leaving the nine-month reserve untouched. In the first year after 2028 I'd keep my paid job and offer those calls only while real customers book; I wouldn't count income until customers pay and costs are deducted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but able to try something with a limit rather than bet the house. I'd like to know whether people book the second visit before describing myself as a businessman.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would those private repairs escape the robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd treat the pilot as a way to test present paid demand, not protection for life after 2031. I won't spend the reserve on machines or promise the family a wage the trial hasn't earned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if permission, insurance or childcare isn't available?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I wouldn't start the Saturday calls. I'd keep the paid job and the work fund intact, rather than leave Rina solving the practical costs of an idea I announced.

say: I'd plan for **both stages**, thinking changes in 2028 and physical robots around 2031.
I'd test **actual customer demand** rather than assume a new job title or small business is automatically safer.
think: My **repair income could shrink** as larger firms automate planning and later ordinary physical fitting.
Our **nine-month reserve** buys a limited trial, not guaranteed customers or permanent safety for either household wage.
do: Start **monthly Saturday repairs** only with written employer permission, confirmed insurance and work within my existing licence and competence.
Cap spending at **300** from the work fund, leaving the reserve intact and agreeing childcare with Rina before starting.
Keep **paid employment** after 2028, accepting trial bookings only while demand exists and counting only paid income after costs.
feel: **Anxious but bounded**, willing to test demand without betting the house or claiming an unearned business income.
S2.quote: I'd like to know whether people book the second visit before describing myself as a businessman.
fieldNote: The **pilot conditions** cover written employer permission, insurance, existing competence, partner agreement and a 300 cap from a separate fund.
He counts **only net receipts** after payment, with uncertain demand and no claim that private physical repairs stay sheltered from robots.

steps.text: Start monthly Saturday repairs only with written employer permission, confirmed insurance, within current licence and skills
Spend at most 300 from work fund, preserve reserve, and agree Saturday childcare with Rina
Keep paid employment after 2028 and count trial income only after payment and costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years lets a family test a small plan properly before making a larger commitment. I'd favour paid apprenticeships and firms that explain the job rather than just advertise a course. I don't think every competent worker needs to become an owner to have a future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My income could still shrink, but I have longer to check actual customer demand before planning changes in 2031. Robots follow around 2034, when I'll be fifty-one, so the private repair idea still isn't a retirement plan or a protected niche. I'd rather discover a weak idea with a three-hundred limit than after spending the reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd seek the same limited monthly Saturday pilot now, starting only with written employer permission, confirmed insurance, licence limits and Rina agreeing childcare. The maximum spend stays three hundred from the separate work fund, with the reserve untouched. In the first year after 2031 I'd continue only if receipts after costs are positive and the family still agrees the time, reviewing the figures quarterly rather than expand because one month went well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less rushed than in the short picture. I could close a trial that doesn't pay without calling myself a failure or dragging the household further into it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you stop even if it earns something?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Rina's shifts or the children's needs make the Saturday impossible, we'd stop or leave that month unbooked. A little extra money doesn't turn the family timetable into something I own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you spend more after a good first quarter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not automatically. I'd compare repeat demand, net receipts and the time it takes, and ask Rina again before any larger plan; I am not committing the reserve or a bigger budget in this picture.

say: I'd test **small household plans** before turning them into a larger commitment.
I'd favour **real paid apprenticeships** without telling every experienced worker to become a business owner.
think: My **income could shrink**, but five years lets me test demand more carefully before planning changes in 2031.
A private repair pilot is **not permanent shelter** from robots around 2034 or a retirement plan at fifty-one.
do: Start **monthly Saturday repairs** only with written employer permission, insurance, existing licence and competence limits, and Rina agreeing childcare.
Cap spending at **300** from the work fund, preserving the reserve rather than committing a larger budget.
Continue after 2031 only with **positive net receipts** and family agreement, reviewing quarterly without automatic expansion.
feel: **Anxious but patient**, able to stop an unprofitable trial without making the household carry a larger gamble.
S3.quote: A little extra money doesn't turn the family timetable into something I own.
fieldNote: The **longer runway** changes evaluation time rather than lifting the spending cap, insurance requirement or need for household agreement.
A **stop rule** covers money and family time, preventing one good month becoming assumed future earnings or automatic expansion.

steps.text: Start monthly Saturday repairs only with written employer permission, confirmed insurance, within current licence and skills
Cap spending at 300 from work fund, protect reserve, and agree childcare with Rina
Continue after 2031 only with positive net receipts and family agreement, reviewing quarterly

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is long enough to make several careful decisions without telling the children my job is safe forever. I'd help them question real apprenticeship offers when they are old enough, including paid hours and who teaches. I'd rather they could read an offer than recite a prediction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own repair work and our money look secure over the next few years with the big change that far away. Thinking AI arrives in 2036 when I'm fifty-three, and robots around 2039 when I'm fifty-six. The children will be eighteen and twenty-four in 2036, but I don't know what help they'll need. I can't assume retirement or a cleared mortgage at fifty-six.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the paid repair job now and wait for the required permissions before any Saturday pilot, using the same insurance, competence, childcare and three-hundred work-fund cap. We'd review actual household income and any trial receipts after costs twice a year, stopping an unaffordable or impractical pilot without touching the reserve. In the first year after 2036 I'd keep paid repair work where offered and review actual hours and bookings monthly before any further commitment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about later work, but comfortable enough with the next few years to keep an ordinary weekend. More time lets me check an idea twice rather than buy a bigger version of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the decade to buy a robot for private jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not without a real price, maintenance costs and repeat paid demand that support the decision. I don't have those figures, and buying one is not part of the three-hundred pilot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could the children's future income fill a household gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't use income they haven't earned in my mortgage budget. They may study, work elsewhere or need help themselves, and I want to discuss their choices without making them our rescue plan.

say: I'd help the children question **real apprenticeship offers**, including paid hours and who will teach.
I'd prefer **reading actual terms** to asking the family to repeat a prediction about safe work.
think: My **near-term repair income** looks secure with the major change a decade away.
I cannot assume **retirement** or a cleared mortgage at fifty-six, or count the children's possible adult earnings as ours.
do: Keep **paid repairs**; require written employer permission, confirmed insurance, licence and competence limits, agreed childcare and a 300 work-fund cap before starting.
Review **net trial receipts** twice yearly, stopping an unaffordable or impractical pilot without using the reserve.
Keep **paid repairs** after 2036 and review actual hours and bookings monthly before further commitments.
feel: **Uneasy about later years**, with near-term security and time to check an idea carefully.
S4.quote: More time lets me check an idea twice rather than buy a bigger version of it.
fieldNote: He retains **the same cap** and household conditions, using extra warning to observe rather than assume capital or guaranteed demand.
He excludes **imaginary child income** and speculative robot purchases, without treating age fifty-six as a guaranteed pension date or debt-free point.

steps.text: Keep the present paid repair job and review actual hours monthly after 2036
Start monthly Saturday repairs only with written employer permission, confirmed insurance, within current licence and skills
Spend at most 300 from work fund, protect reserve, and agree childcare with Rina
Review net trial receipts twice yearly and stop an unaffordable or impractical pilot

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the thinking change starts quickly and physical robots around 2031 could squeeze both our wages. Honest paid hours and practical training that doesn't cost the weekly wage would help. For any small outside-work trial I'd need clear employer and insurance terms, not a lecture about becoming entrepreneurial.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask the family before calling somebody's spare Saturday an unused business opportunity. Rina already works hard, and the children don't have another father on standby. A small plan is only small if the family can actually carry it.

headlineQuote: A small plan is only small if the family can actually carry it.
portrait: Marco is a **43-year-old licensed electrician** with a vocational certificate and ordinary repair experience, without specialist or managerial status.
He has **nine months saved**, higher pay, many nearby firms, a mortgage and two schoolchildren with bakery-working wife Rina.
He uses **AI occasionally** after colleague testing, preferring a paid proven trial over being the first person to discover every error.
His **Saturday repair pilot** requires permission, insurance, competence limits, family agreement and a separate capped fund rather than an assumed business wage.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could bring physical robots around 2031 that squeeze both household wages before careful adjustment.
whatWouldHelp: **Honest paid hours** and practical teaching without lost weekly wages would support adjustment.
Clear **employer and insurance terms** would make a limited outside-work trial reviewable.
